title: A ladder of song
hook: the niggun climbs from sadness to joy to stillness

segments.voice: Yesterday, clothes remember: the long coat and the fur hat holding a memory of old Eastern Europe. Did you touch one thing you wore and recall where it came from? A new week begins. Day one thousand two hundred five.

Yai, dai, bim, bam. What do those syllables mean? Nothing. You won't find them in a dictionary. And yet a group of Hasidim can sing them over and over, slow at first, almost sad. Then the tune picks up. Hands drum on whatever is nearby. Somebody stands. And then, somehow, it slows again, softer and softer, until the singers are only breathing. Nobody announces any of this. The song leads them there. Hasidim have a name for that kind of song, and a picture for where it takes you. Today's word.
screen: `YAI, DAI, BIM, BAM.` → `NO DICTIONARY HAS THEM.` → `THE SONG LEADS.`

segments.voice: A ladder of song. The Hebrew word is niggun, a melody, and in Hasidic life it often means a tune sung without words. Turn it four ways. First, why no words. Words can only say what they say. Hasidic teachers describe the wordless tune as reaching past language, to a place the heart knows but can't name. A syllable like yai has nothing to argue with. Second, the climb. Some niggunim move in stages. They begin in longing, sometimes close to sadness. They rise into joy. And some end in stillness, a quiet the song has earned. That's the ladder: down where you are, up toward God, and then a rung where even the song stops. In Genesis, Jacob dreams of "a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven." The niggun is a ladder you can sing. Third, an old precedent. In the book of Kings, the prophet Elisha needs to hear God's word, and he asks for music first: "But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the LORD came upon him." Music came before the message. Fourth, how it lives. Courts keep their own niggunim, some said to come from their founding rebbes, and pass them down like the coats from yesterday. Tradition says some Hasidic leaders composed tunes, and some adopted folk melodies they heard around them, believing a holy spark was waiting inside. A shepherd's song could become a prayer. On an ordinary evening, a niggun asks only that you hum.
screen: `A TUNE WITHOUT WORDS.` · `LONGING, JOY, STILLNESS.` · `BRING ME A MINSTREL.` · `A SHEPHERD'S SONG, LIFTED.` · then, large: `A LADDER OF SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum a slow tune. Any tune you know, or none at all, just a few notes on one syllable, like yai or dai. Start low and slow, a little sad if that's where you are. Hum it a few times. Let it lift on its own, a little brighter, a little faster, if it wants to. Then let it slow down again, softer, until you're only humming on the breath. Then stop, and stay in the quiet the tune left behind. If you're somewhere you can't make a sound, hum it inside. The bell holds the time.
A ladder of song. The niggun, a Hasidic melody often sung without words, that can climb from longing to joy to stillness. Today's word.
Your line: a ladder of song. Today, when you're waiting, walking or washing a dish, hum one slow line under your breath, and notice where it takes you. Day one thousand two hundred five.

howItsDone: Hasidim sing niggunim at the Shabbat table, at a rebbe's gathering, before prayer and at celebrations; a tune is often repeated many times, slowly building and then quieting.

notes: The three-stage shape (longing, joy, stillness) is presented as true of 'some niggunim', following the outline; please confirm.
